# Polynomial Automorphisms and the Preservation of Structural Properties

## Introduction

Given a group $G$, one may consider a special class of automorphisms known as **polynomial automorphisms**—maps of $G$ into itself that arise from group-theoretic expressions (words) in the elements of $G$, subject to appropriate conditions ensuring bijectivity. These automorphisms need not exhaust the full automorphism group $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$; rather, they typically generate a proper subgroup, which we denote by $\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{poly}}(G) \leq \mathrm{Aut}(G)$.

This distinguished subgroup $\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{poly}}(G)$ captures automorphisms with a specific algebraic or combinatorial origin, and it is natural to ask how the structural properties of $G$ itself are reflected in the structure of this subgroup. The central result addressed here demonstrates a striking correspondence: certain fundamental classifications of $G$—namely nilpotency and metabelian-ness—are inherited by $\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{poly}}(G)$.

## The Subgroup Generated by Polynomial Automorphisms

For a group $G$, the polynomial automorphisms form a generating set for a subgroup of $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$. Formally,
$$
\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{poly}}(G) := \langle \varphi \in \mathrm{Aut}(G) : \varphi \text{ is a polynomial automorphism} \rangle.
$$
This subgroup is, by construction, the smallest subgroup of $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$ containing all such polynomial maps. The significance of isolating this subgroup lies in the fact that polynomial automorphisms often arise naturally from the internal algebraic structure of $G$—for instance, via conjugation-like expressions, commutator manipulations, or other polynomial identities intrinsic to the group law. Consequently, $\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{poly}}(G)$ serves as a meaningful algebraic invariant that encodes how the internal structure of $G$ manifests itself at the level of automorphisms.

## Main Results

The principal theorem governing this construction can be stated as follows:

**Theorem (Nilpotent Case).** If $G$ is a nilpotent group, then the subgroup $\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{poly}}(G)$ of $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$ generated by all polynomial automorphisms is itself nilpotent.

**Theorem (Metabelian Case).** If $G$ is a metabelian group, then the subgroup $\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{poly}}(G)$ of $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$ generated by all polynomial automorphisms is itself metabelian.

Together, these two results establish a unifying principle: **the classification of $G$ as nilpotent or metabelian is transferred to $\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{poly}}(G)$**. In other words, passing from $G$ to the polynomial automorphism subgroup does not increase the structural complexity of the group in either of these senses—nilpotency class and derived length (in the metabelian case) behave predictably under this construction, at least insofar as the property itself (rather than the precise invariant, such as the nilpotency class) is preserved.

## Structural Interpretation

The heart of the matter is that $\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{poly}}(G)$, despite being defined as a subgroup of the automorphism group $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$—a group that can be considerably larger and more complicated than $G$ itself—remains constrained by the same broad structural classification as $G$. This is a nontrivial phenomenon: in general, subgroups of automorphism groups of nilpotent or metabelian groups need not themselves be nilpotent or metabelian. The special role played by polynomial automorphisms is precisely what allows this inheritance of structure to occur.

The proof strategy in each case exploits the polynomial nature of the generating automorphisms directly: because each generator of $\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{poly}}(G)$ is expressible via a polynomial expression in the elements of $G$, the relations satisfied by these automorphisms mirror the relations satisfied within $G$ itself. In the nilpotent case, this allows one to bound the length of the descending or ascending central series of $\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{poly}}(G)$ in terms of data intrinsic to $G$'s own nilpotency class. In the metabelian case, an analogous argument shows that the derived subgroup of $\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{poly}}(G)$ is abelian, mirroring the defining property of metabelian groups, precisely because the commutators of polynomial automorphisms can be controlled via the commutator structure of $G$.

## Conclusion

In summary, this body of results establishes a robust correspondence between the algebraic classification of a group $G$—whether nilpotent or metabelian—and the corresponding classification of the subgroup $\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{poly}}(G) \leq \mathrm{Aut}(G)$ generated by its polynomial automorphisms. This correspondence reveals that polynomial automorphisms, rather than being an arbitrary or unstructured subset of the full automorphism group, form a subgroup whose complexity is tightly governed by the structural properties of the underlying group $G$. Such a result underscores the deep interplay between the internal algebraic structure of a group and the automorphisms it admits, particularly those automorphisms arising from polynomial expressions native to the group itself.

# Polynomial Automorphisms and Structural Preservation in Group Theory

## Introduction

The study of automorphism groups has long occupied a central position in the structural theory of groups. Among the various classes of automorphisms that arise naturally in this context, polynomial automorphisms represent a particularly rich and tractable family, characterized by their compatibility with the underlying algebraic operations of the group in a manner analogous to polynomial maps in classical algebra. This work is devoted to a systematic examination of the subgroup generated by all such polynomial automorphisms of a given group, with particular attention to how the structural properties of the original group are reflected in, and preserved by, this associated subgroup.

## Background and Motivation

Given a group $G$, an automorphism $\varphi \in \mathrm{Aut}(G)$ is said to be *polynomial* if it can be expressed, in an appropriate sense, as a polynomial function on $G$—that is, as a composition built from the group operations, inner automorphisms, and other canonically defined maps, satisfying a bounded degree condition relative to the lower central or derived series of $G$. The collection of all polynomial automorphisms need not itself form a subgroup of $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$ in general, since the composition of polynomial maps of bounded degree can, in principle, generate automorphisms of unbounded complexity. It is therefore natural to consider instead the subgroup $P(G) \leq \mathrm{Aut}(G)$ generated by all polynomial automorphisms, and to ask what structural constraints on $G$ are inherited by $P(G)$.

This question is motivated by several considerations. First, from the perspective of the general theory of automorphism groups, it is of intrinsic interest to determine which subgroups of $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$ retain the qualitative structural features of $G$ itself. Second, polynomial automorphisms arise naturally in the study of nilpotent and solvable groups, where the lower central series and derived series provide a graded or filtered structure against which polynomiality can be measured. Finally, understanding the behavior of $P(G)$ provides a bridge between the combinatorial group theory of automorphisms and the more algebraic theory of graded Lie rings associated to $G$ via its central series, since polynomial automorphisms typically induce well-behaved maps on these associated graded objects.

## Main Results

The principal result of this work establishes a precise correspondence between the structural class of $G$ and that of $P(G)$:

**Theorem.** Let $G$ be a group, and let $P(G)$ denote the subgroup of $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$ generated by all polynomial automorphisms of $G$. Then:

1. If $G$ is nilpotent, then $P(G)$ is nilpotent.
2. If $G$ is metabelian, then $P(G)$ is metabelian.

The significance of this theorem lies in the fact that it demonstrates a genuine preservation phenomenon: the polynomial automorphism construction, despite its potential to introduce automorphisms of considerable combinatorial complexity, does not escape the structural class to which $G$ belongs. In particular, the nilpotency class or the metabelian structure of $G$ constrains—via the polynomiality condition—the corresponding structure of $P(G)$, even though $P(G)$ is a subgroup of the full automorphism group $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$, which may itself be far from nilpotent or metabelian.

## Discussion of the Nilpotent Case

The proof strategy in the nilpotent case proceeds by exploiting the compatibility between polynomial automorphisms and the lower central series $\gamma_1(G) \geq \gamma_2(G) \geq \cdots \geq \gamma_c(G) \geq \gamma_{c+1}(G) = 1$ of a nilpotent group $G$ of class $c$. A key observation is that any polynomial automorphism $\varphi$ of bounded degree $d$ induces, upon passage to the associated graded Lie ring $L(G) = \bigoplus_{i=1}^{c} \gamma_i(G)/\gamma_{i+1}(G)$, a map that respects the graded structure up to controlled degree shifts. This allows one to organize the generators of $P(G)$ according to their effect on the graded pieces of $L(G)$, and to show that commutators of sufficiently many polynomial automorphisms act trivially on $G$ modulo terms of arbitrarily high nilpotency class. Since $G$ has finite nilpotency class $c$, this commutator vanishing translates directly into an upper bound on the nilpotency class of $P(G)$, expressed as a function of $c$ and the degrees of the generating polynomial automorphisms.

## Discussion of the Metabelian Case

The metabelian case requires a somewhat different approach, since metabelian groups are not naturally filtered by a central series but rather by the derived series $G \geq G' \geq G'' = 1$. Here, the analysis centers on how polynomial automorphisms interact with the abelian normal subgroup $G'$ and the abelian quotient $G/G'$. A polynomial automorphism of $G$ restricts to an automorphism of $G'$ and induces an automorphism of $G/G'$, and the polynomiality condition ensures that the resulting action on $G'$, when $G/G'$ acts by conjugation, remains compatible with the module structure of $G'$ over the group ring of $G/G'$. This compatibility is sufficient to show that the derived subgroup of $P(G)$ acts trivially on the associated graded pieces determined by $G'$ and $G/G'$, from which metabelianness of $P(G)$ follows by a direct commutator computation.

## Conclusion

The results presented here contribute to a broader program of understanding how automorphism-theoretic constructions interact with the structural hierarchy of groups classified by nilpotency and solvability. By showing that the subgroup generated by polynomial automorphisms preserves both nilpotency and metabelian structure, this work establishes polynomial automorphisms as a natural and well-behaved tool for studying the automorphism groups of structured groups, opening avenues for further investigation into finer invariants—such as precise bounds on nilpotency class or derived length—as well as potential generalizations to broader classes of solvable groups.

# Polynomial Automorphisms and Nilpotent/Solvable Groups

## Setup and Definitions

Let $G$ be a group. Recall that a **polynomial map** $f: G \to G$ is one built up from the identity map and constant maps using the group operations (multiplication and inversion), i.e., $f(x)$ is given by a word in $x$ and elements of $G$. A **polynomial automorphism** is a polynomial map that is also a bijection (equivalently, an automorphism of $G$ that can be written as such a word map).

The relevant group is:
$$\mathrm{PAut}(G) = \{\varphi \in \mathrm{Aut}(G) : \varphi \text{ is a polynomial map}\}$$

This is a subgroup of $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$, and it contains all **inner automorphisms**, since $\mathrm{Inn}(g)(x) = gxg^{-1}$ is manifestly polynomial.

## Main Theorem

**Theorem.** If $G$ is nilpotent of class $c$, then $\mathrm{PAut}(G)$ is nilpotent of class $\le c$ (or a similar bound in terms of $c$). If $G$ is metabelian (solvable of derived length 2), then $\mathrm{PAut}(G)$ is metabelian.

## Proof Strategy

The key idea is to bound the **degree** of a polynomial automorphism using the nilpotency/solvability of $G$, and to show that the polynomial automorphism group inherits the corresponding commutator identities.

### Step 1: Degree filtration

Define the degree of a polynomial map inductively:
- Constant maps and the identity map have degree $\le 1$.
- If $f, g$ have degree $\le m, n$, then $fg$ (pointwise product) and $f^{-1}$ (pointwise inverse) have degree $\le m+n$.

Let $\mathrm{Pol}_d(G)$ denote polynomial maps of degree $\le d$. Because $G$ is nilpotent of class $c$, all $(c+1)$-fold commutators vanish:
$$[x_1, \dots, x_{c+1}] = 1 \text{ for all } x_i \in G.$$

**Key Lemma.** Every polynomial map $f \in \mathrm{Pol}_d(G)$ can be written using the **Hall–Petresco identity** (or via repeated use of commutator collection) as
$$f(x) = x^{n} \cdot c_2(x)^{\binom{d}{2}}\cdots$$
in terms of $x$ and higher commutators involving constants from $G$; because $G$ is nilpotent of class $c$, terms of "commutator weight" $> c$ vanish. This effectively **truncates** the polynomial map data to a bounded amount of information (the terms of weight $\le c$), controlled by finitely many group elements from $G$.

### Step 2: Commutators of polynomial automorphisms

Given $\varphi, \psi \in \mathrm{PAut}(G)$, the commutator $[\varphi,\psi] = \varphi\psi\varphi^{-1}\psi^{-1}$ acts on $x \in G$ by:
$$[\varphi,\psi](x) = \varphi(\psi(\varphi^{-1}(\psi^{-1}(x))))$$

Since $\varphi, \psi$ are polynomial in $x$ (with parameters from $G$), $[\varphi,\psi](x)$ is again a polynomial expression in $x$. The crucial point is to show:

**Claim:** If $\varphi$ fixes the quotient $G/\gamma_k(G)$ (acting trivially modulo the $k$-th term of the lower central series) then $[\varphi, \psi]$ acts trivially modulo $\gamma_{k+1}(G)$ **when $\psi$ is arbitrary**, or more precisely, the commutators of $\mathrm{PAut}(G)$ interact with the filtration
$$\mathrm{PAut}(G) = A_0 \ge A_1 \ge A_2 \ge \cdots$$
where $A_i$ consists of automorphisms inducing the identity on $\gamma_j(G)/\gamma_{j+1}(G)$ for $j \le i$, satisfying:
$$[A_i, A_j] \subseteq A_{i+j}.$$

This is proven by direct computation: writing $\varphi(x) = x \cdot u(x)$ where $u(x) \in \gamma_{i+1}(G)$ modulo higher terms (since $\varphi \in A_i$ means $\varphi$ is "close to identity" up to level $i$), and using the standard commutator collection formulas in nilpotent groups (Hall–Petresco/Lazard correspondence) to track how these correction terms multiply.

### Step 3: Termination

Since $G$ has nilpotency class $c$, the lower central series terminates: $\gamma_{c+1}(G) = 1$. Hence $A_c = 1$ (any automorphism inducing the identity on all graded pieces up to level $c$ must be the identity, since $\gamma_{c+1} = 1$). Thus the filtration
$$\mathrm{PAut}(G) = A_0 \supseteq A_1 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq A_c = 1$$
gives, via $[A_i, A_j] \subseteq A_{i+j}$, that $\mathrm{PAut}(G)$ is nilpotent of class bounded in terms of $c$ (a standard fact: a group with a filtration satisfying $[A_i,A_j]\subseteq A_{i+j}$ and $A_{c}=1$ is nilpotent of class at most a function of $c$, often $c$ itself or close to it after normalizing indices).

## The Metabelian Case

If $G$ is metabelian, $G'' = 1$, i.e., $G' = [G,G]$ is abelian. Any polynomial automorphism $\varphi$ preserves $G'$ (it is a fully characteristic/verbal subgroup), so we get a homomorphism:
$$\mathrm{PAut}(G) \to \mathrm{Aut}(G/G') \times \mathrm{Aut}(G')$$
via restriction to the abelian pieces $G/G'$ and $G'$. Let $K$ be the kernel — automorphisms acting trivially on both $G/G'$ and $G'$.

- The image in $\mathrm{Aut}(G/G')$ is **abelian** because $G/G'$ is abelian, and polynomial automorphisms restricted to an abelian group act by "degree $\le 1$" data (since higher commutators vanish identically), forcing the induced automorphisms to commute (they act as affine/linear-type maps whose composition is commutative in the relevant coordinates, by a direct computation analogous to Step 2 with $c=1$).
- Similarly, the action on $G'$ (abelian) forces $K$ itself to be abelian by the same reasoning as the nilpotent case with $c = 1$.

Hence we get:
$$1 \to K \to \mathrm{PAut}(G) \to Q \to 1$$
with $K$ abelian and $Q$ abelian (a subgroup of $\mathrm{Aut}(G/G')\times \mathrm{Aut}(G')$ built from commuting polynomial data), so $\mathrm{PAut}(G)$ is **metabelian**.

## Conclusion

In both cases, the strategy is:
1. Use the (lower central or derived) series of $G$ to filter $\mathrm{PAut}(G)$.
2. Show the filtration is compatible with commutators: $[A_i, A_j] \subseteq A_{i+j}$ (nilpotent case) or that consecutive quotients are abelian (solvable case), using that polynomial maps are literally built from the group operations, so their commutators can be computed via the same identities that make $G$ nilpotent/metabelian.
3. Conclude termination of the filtration from the corresponding termination in $G$, giving nilpotency (resp. metabelian-ness) of $\mathrm{PAut}(G)$. $\blacksquare$

# Subgroups Generated by Polynomial Automorphisms: Nilpotent and Metabelian Cases

This question relates to the structure theory of the **Cremona group** and, more specifically, to **groups of polynomial automorphisms** of affine space $\mathbb{A}^n$ (i.e., $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{A}^n)$), as well as to results about subgroups of such automorphism groups that are nilpotent or metabelian.

## Key Structural Results

### 1. Tits Alternative-type Behavior

Polynomial automorphism groups (and Cremona groups more generally) satisfy a **Tits alternative**: subgroups either contain a nonabelian free subgroup, or are "small" in a precise algebraic sense (virtually solvable, or built from simpler pieces). This dichotomy forces nilpotent and metabelian subgroups into very restricted forms.

### 2. Nilpotent Subgroups

For nilpotent subgroups $G \leq \mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{A}^n)$ (or more generally the Cremona group $\mathrm{Bir}(X)$):

- **Triangularizability**: A nilpotent subgroup of polynomial automorphisms can often be conjugated (or shown to act) so that it stabilizes a flag of subvarieties, reflecting the classical fact that unipotent/nilpotent linear groups are triangularizable (Lie–Kolchin type phenomena extend to this birational setting).
- **Bounded degree growth**: Elements of a nilpotent subgroup exhibit **polynomial degree growth** under iteration (the degree of the $n$-th iterate grows polynomially in $n$), rather than exponential growth typical of "positive entropy" automorphisms. This follows from the dynamical degree theory: nilpotent groups cannot contain elements of positive entropy.
- Concretely, in $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{A}^2)$, nilpotent subgroups are conjugate into the group of **triangular (de Jonquières-type) automorphisms**, or are virtually abelian coming from linear parts.

### 3. Metabelian Subgroups

Metabelian groups (solvable of derived length $\leq 2$) form the next layer:

- They still fall under the **solvable case** of the Tits alternative, hence act with **zero entropy** — all dynamical degrees equal 1, meaning no element can have exponential complexity growth.
- Structurally, metabelian subgroups often arise as **extensions of translations/torus actions by abelian automorphisms**, e.g., subgroups of the affine group $\mathrm{Aff}_n$, or the semi-direct product coming from the standard "elementary/triangular" automorphisms $(x_1,\dots,x_n) \mapsto (a_1x_1+b_1(x_2,\dots,x_n),\ldots)$.
- In dimension 2, the classical **Jung–van der Kulk theorem** describing $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{A}^2)$ as an amalgamated product of the affine and triangular groups implies that metabelian (and more generally solvable) subgroups are conjugate into the triangular subgroup or are extensions of finite groups by such — using Bass–Serre theory on groups acting on trees (the amalgam structure).

### 4. Role of the Amalgamated Product / Bass–Serre Theory

Since $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{A}^2) \cong A *_C J$ (affine group amalgamated with the triangular group over their intersection), general structure theorems for subgroups of amalgams apply:

- Any subgroup **not conjugate into a factor** acts on the associated Bass–Serre tree without a fixed point, hence (unless it's a specific small case) contains a **free subgroup** — consistent with Tits alternative.
- **Nilpotent and metabelian subgroups**, lacking free subgroups (nilpotent groups never contain $F_2$; metabelian groups can't contain $F_2$ either since $F_2$ isn't solvable), must therefore **fix a point of the tree**, meaning they are conjugate into $A$ or $J$ (the affine or triangular subgroup) — or fix an edge, landing in the intersection $C$.

## Summary

| Property | Nilpotent Subgroups | Metabelian Subgroups |
|---|---|---|
| Dynamical degree | All degrees = 1 (zero entropy) | All degrees = 1 (zero entropy) |
| Free subgroups | None | None |
| Tree action (dim 2) | Fixes a vertex → conjugate into $A$ or $J$ | Same, but more possibilities (extensions) |
| Structural form | Conjugate to triangular or affine unipotent group | Conjugate into triangular/affine group, or built as an extension of translations by an abelian group |

**In short:** nilpotent and metabelian subgroups of polynomial automorphism groups are "geometrically simple" — they act with zero entropy, avoid free subgroups, and (via Bass–Serre theory in low dimension) can be conjugated into the standard affine or triangular subgroups, reflecting the general principle that solvability/nilpotency forces polynomial automorphisms into essentially linear or triangular normal forms.

# Abstract

Let $G$ be a group and let $\operatorname{Aut}_p(G)$ denote the subgroup of polynomial automorphisms of $G$—that is, automorphisms whose action on elements can be expressed via fixed polynomial expressions in the group's structural invariants (e.g., commutators, central series representatives, or coordinates arising from a fixed generating set). This paper investigates the extent to which such polynomial automorphism subgroups respect and preserve fundamental solvability-type structural properties of the ambient group, focusing specifically on nilpotency and metabelianness.

We first establish that if $G$ is a nilpotent group of class $c$, then any subgroup $H \leq \operatorname{Aut}_p(G)$ acts in a manner compatible with the lower central series of $G$: each polynomial automorphism in $H$ stabilizes the terms $\gamma_i(G)$ setwise and induces polynomial automorphisms on the associated graded pieces $\gamma_i(G)/\gamma_{i+1}(G)$. As a consequence, we show that the semidirect product $G \rtimes H$ remains nilpotent of bounded class whenever $H$ satisfies a mild degree-boundedness condition on its polynomial degree, and we compute explicit bounds relating the nilpotency class of $G \rtimes H$ to that of $G$ and the maximal polynomial degree occurring in $H$.

Second, we turn to metabelian groups, where $G' \leq Z(G)$-type conditions are replaced by the weaker requirement $G'' = 1$. We prove that polynomial automorphisms necessarily preserve the derived series up to the second term: any $\phi \in \operatorname{Aut}_p(G)$ satisfies $\phi(G') = G'$, and moreover the induced action on the abelianization $G/G'$ extends canonically to a polynomial automorphism of the associated metabelian quotient. This allows us to construct a functorial correspondence between polynomial automorphism subgroups of $G$ and those of $G^{ab} = G/G'$, clarifying how metabelian structure descends through polynomial automorphisms.

Combining these results, we obtain a unified structural theorem: for $G$ lying in the variety of nilpotent-by-metabelian groups, every finitely generated subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}_p(G)$ preserves this variety membership under semidirect extension. We illustrate the theorem with applications to free nilpotent groups, wreath products, and groups arising from polynomial mappings in algebraic geometry (in particular, tame and wild automorphisms of polynomial rings acting on associated nilpotent Lie rings via the Lazard correspondence). Our results provide new tools for constructing and classifying nilpotent and metabelian groups equipped with rich automorphism structure, and suggest further directions concerning solvable groups of higher derived length under polynomial automorphism actions.

# Theorem: Group Structure and Closure Properties of Polynomial Automorphism Groups

## Statement

Let $G$ be a group, and consider the set of **polynomial maps** on $G$ (maps expressible via a fixed word using group operations and constants) together with the subset of these that are **bijective automorphisms** (polynomial automorphisms). The theorem relates algebraic structure of $G$ to closure/topological properties of its associated transformation group:

**Theorem.** Let $G$ be a group.

1. If $G$ is **nilpotent** (of class $c$), then the group $P(G)$ of polynomial permutations of $G$ (permutations induced by polynomial maps in the sense above) is a **subgroup** of $\mathrm{Sym}(G)$, and moreover $P(G)$ is closed in $\mathrm{Sym}(G)$ under the topology of pointwise convergence (i.e., it equals its own closure). Nilpotency guarantees that inverses and compositions of polynomial maps remain polynomial, so the set of polynomial bijections is automatically a group.

2. If $G$ is **metabelian** (solvable of derived length 2), then polynomial maps need not compose or invert within the polynomial class, but the set of polynomial *permutations* still forms a group **after closure**: the topological closure $\overline{P(G)}$ of the polynomial permutations in $\mathrm{Sym}(G)$ is a group, even though $P(G)$ itself may fail to be a group. Equivalently, metabelian groups guarantee that the failure of closure under composition/inversion is "repaired" by passing to limits, so that
$$
\overline{P(G)} \le \mathrm{Sym}(G)
$$
is always a subgroup, though $P(G)$ itself may not be.

## Interpretation

- **Nilpotent case:** strong algebraic structure (commutators of bounded depth vanish) forces polynomial bijections to already form a group — no closure needed.
- **Metabelian case:** weaker structure (only two-step solvability) is not enough to guarantee this on the nose, but is exactly enough to guarantee it *in the closure*, revealing a precise correspondence between the **derived length / nilpotency class** of $G$ and the **degree of "defect"** in $P(G)$ being a group, measured by how much closure is required to repair it.

This illustrates a general theme: the more one climbs the solvable/nilpotent hierarchy, the more one needs to pass to closures (topological limits) to recover group-theoretic closure properties of polynomial transformation semigroups — nilpotent groups needing none, metabelian groups needing exactly the pointwise-convergence closure.
